title: Expose your GenAI work as an API with FastAPI
summary: Turn your GenAI scripts into a real web service with FastAPI: define endpoints, type your request and response with Pydantic models, and run it with uvicorn.
objectives: Explain why exposing GenAI work as an HTTP API matters for production
Create a FastAPI app with GET and POST endpoints
Type request and response bodies with Pydantic models for automatic validation
Run the app locally with uvicorn and explore the auto-generated docs
Call a Claude model from inside an endpoint and return a structured response
Use async endpoints so the server handles many requests concurrently

quiz.q: What does FastAPI give you automatically when you type your endpoints with Pydantic models?
options: Request validation, JSON serialisation, and interactive API docs
quiz.why: FastAPI uses the Pydantic types on your function to validate incoming JSON, serialise responses, and generate interactive OpenAPI docs at /docs — all for free.

quiz.q: Which tool runs a FastAPI app?
quiz.why: FastAPI is an ASGI framework, so you run it with an ASGI server such as uvicorn, e.g. uvicorn main:app --reload.

quiz.q: Why declare a request body as a Pydantic model rather than reading raw JSON?
options: FastAPI then validates and parses the body for you and rejects bad input with a clear 422 error
It is required to return JSON
quiz.why: Typing the body as a Pydantic model means FastAPI parses and validates it automatically, returning a helpful 422 error if the client sends the wrong shape.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of making an endpoint that calls an LLM an async def endpoint?
options: The server can handle other requests while this one waits on the model, improving throughput
It removes the need for uvicorn
quiz.why: An LLM call is I/O-bound; an async endpoint lets the event loop serve other requests during the wait instead of blocking a worker.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what does the @app.post("/path") decorator do?
quiz.answer: It registers the function below it as the handler for HTTP POST requests to that URL path on your FastAPI app.
quiz.why: The decorator wires a URL and HTTP method to your Python function so FastAPI routes matching requests to it.

quiz.q: Where can you try your API in the browser without writing a client?
quiz.answer: At the auto-generated interactive docs, served by default at /docs (Swagger UI), or /redoc.
quiz.why: FastAPI builds an OpenAPI schema from your types and serves Swagger UI at /docs so you can call endpoints from the browser.

resources.label: FastAPI — Tutorial: First Steps & Request Body

body_markdown:
## From script to service

A script that summarises a document is useful to you. A **service** that summarises a document is useful to everyone — your colleagues, a web app, another microservice, a CI/CD job. The difference is an **API**: an HTTP endpoint others can call over the network. As a cloud engineer you already deploy and secure services; now you'll build one that wraps your GenAI work.

**FastAPI** is the standard modern way to do this in Python. It's fast, it's typed, and it turns your Pydantic models into automatic validation and documentation. Let's build one.

## Your first endpoint

Install it and write a tiny app.

```bash
pip install "fastapi[standard]" uvicorn
```

```python
# main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}
```

The `@app.get("/health")` decorator registers the function as the handler for `GET /health`. Returning a dict is enough — FastAPI serialises it to JSON for you.

## Typed requests and responses

Real endpoints accept input. Declare the shape with a **Pydantic model** and FastAPI validates it automatically: the right fields, the right types, or a clear `422` error back to the caller.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class SummariseRequest(BaseModel):
    text: str
    max_words: int = 50

class SummariseResponse(BaseModel):
    summary: str

@app.post("/summarise", response_model=SummariseResponse)
def summarise(req: SummariseRequest):
    ...
```

By typing `req: SummariseRequest`, FastAPI parses and validates the JSON body. By setting `response_model`, it validates and documents what you send back. You get correctness and documentation for free.

## Running it with uvicorn

FastAPI is an **ASGI** app, so you run it with an ASGI server — **uvicorn**.

```bash
uvicorn main:app --reload
```

Here `main` is the file and `app` is the FastAPI object. `--reload` restarts on code changes during development. Now open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs` — FastAPI built interactive **Swagger UI** from your types, so you can call your endpoints from the browser with no client code.

## Calling Claude from an endpoint

Now wire in the model. Because an LLM call waits on the network, make the endpoint **async** so the server can serve other requests during the wait.

```python
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

client = AsyncAnthropic()

@app.post("/summarise", response_model=SummariseResponse)
async def summarise(req: SummariseRequest):
    msg = await client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=300,
        system=f"Summarise in at most {req.max_words} words.",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": req.text}],
    )
    return SummariseResponse(summary=msg.content[0].text)
```

Notice the system prompt is a **top-level** field and the user text is a message — that's the Anthropic Messages API shape. The same service pattern fronts a model on Amazon Bedrock or Azure equally well.

## Why this is production-shaped

You now have a typed, documented, async HTTP service. From here it's familiar cloud territory: put it behind a gateway, add an API key dependency, log requests, and containerise it (next lessons). You've turned a notebook experiment into something deployable.

## Your task

Build a FastAPI app with a `POST /summarise` endpoint that takes `text` and `max_words`, calls a Claude model asynchronously, and returns a typed `SummariseResponse`. Run it with uvicorn and test it from the `/docs` page.

slides.narration: In the last lesson you learned to make many model calls fast. Now we make your work usable by others. Right now your GenAI code is a script only you can run. In this lesson we wrap it in a real web service using FastAPI, so a web app, a colleague, or another microservice can call it over H T T P. You'll define endpoints, type them, and run the whole thing with uvicorn.

slides.title: From script to service
bullets: A script helps you. A service helps everyone.
An API is an HTTP endpoint others can call.
You already deploy and secure services.
FastAPI is the modern Python way.
slides.narration: Here's the shift in mindset. A script that summarises a document is useful to you alone. A service that summarises a document is useful to everyone, your colleagues, a front-end app, a CI job, another microservice. The thing that makes that leap is an A P I, an H T T P endpoint others can call over the network. As a cloud engineer you already deploy and secure services every day. FastAPI lets you build one that wraps your GenAI work, and it's the standard modern way to do it in Python.

slides.title: Your first endpoint
bullets: pip install fastapi and uvicorn.
@app.get("/health") registers a handler.
Return a dict — FastAPI makes it JSON.
Decorator wires URL + method to your function.
slides.narration: Let's build the smallest possible app. After installing FastAPI and uvicorn, you create a FastAPI object called app. Then you write a function and put the decorator at app dot get, slash health, above it. That decorator registers your function as the handler for a G E T request to slash health. And notice you just return a Python dictionary. FastAPI serialises it to Jason for you automatically. That's a working endpoint in five lines.

slides.title: Typed requests with Pydantic
bullets: Declare the body shape as a Pydantic model.
FastAPI validates the incoming JSON for you.
Bad input gets a clear 422 error.
response_model documents what you return.
slides.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class SummariseRequest(BaseModel):
    text: str
    max_words: int = 50
slides.narration: Real endpoints take input, and here's where FastAPI shines. You declare the shape of the request body as a Pydantic model, a class with typed fields. When you type your function's argument as that model, FastAPI parses and validates the incoming Jason for you. If the caller sends the wrong fields or wrong types, they get a clear four-two-two error explaining exactly what's wrong. Set a response model too, and FastAPI validates and documents what you send back. You get correctness and docs for free.

slides.title: Run it with uvicorn
bullets: FastAPI is an ASGI app.
uvicorn main:app --reload runs it.
main is the file, app is the object.
--reload restarts on code changes.
slides.narration: FastAPI is what's called an A S G I app, so you run it with an A S G I server, and the usual choice is uvicorn. You type uvicorn, then main colon app. Main is your file name, app is the FastAPI object inside it. The dash dash reload flag restarts the server whenever you change your code, which is lovely while developing. Run that, and your service is live on your machine.

FastAPI has read the Pydantic types on your endpoints and built a full interactive documentation page, called Swagger U I, automatically. You can fill in a request and call your endpoint right there in the browser, with no client code at all. For testing and for sharing with teammates, this is fantastic. There's a second view at slash redoc if you prefer it.

slides.title: Call Claude from an endpoint
bullets: Make the endpoint async — the model call waits.
await client.messages.create(...).
system is top-level; user text is a message.
Works the same fronting Bedrock or Azure.
slides.code:
@app.post("/summarise",
          response_model=SummariseResponse)
async def summarise(req: SummariseRequest):
    msg = await client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=300,
        system="Summarise concisely.",
        messages=[{"role": "user",
                   "content": req.text}],
    )
    return SummariseResponse(
        summary=msg.content[0].text)
slides.narration: Now we wire in the model. Because the call waits on the network, we make the endpoint async def and await client dot messages dot create. We're using a Sonnet model here for a good balance of quality and speed on a summarisation task. Look closely at the shape: the system prompt is a top-level field, and the user's text goes in the messages list with role user. That's the Anthropic Messages A P I. Making the endpoint async means while this request waits on the model, your server happily serves other callers. And this exact pattern fronts a model on Bedrock or Azure just as well.

You add an A P I key check as a dependency, you log requests, you put it behind a gateway, and you containerise it, which is exactly where this module is heading. You've taken a notebook experiment and turned it into something genuinely deployable.
